📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished.

Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past.

Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth.

Normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged.

One of the most striking examples is found in the Grand Canyon, where rocks separated by hundreds of millions of years sit directly on top of one another, as if some force or phenomenon removed the layers that geologists would expect to see in between. This enormous gap in Earth's geological timeline is part of the phenomenon known as the Great Unconformity.

According to recent reports, it's not just the Grand Canyon. Similar gaps have been identified across Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia. Depending on the location, the missing interval ranges from approximately 200 million years to more than a billion years.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out," study lead author Santosh Dhungana said in a statement.

According to recent reports, "The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance.".

In a fresh study published in the journal Nature, Dhungana and study co-author Nicolas Flament investigated whether activity far below Earth's surface was to blame.

Using computer models, they explored how the slow circulation of hot rock within Earth's mantle may have affected the continents over hundreds of millions of years.

Recent findings suggest that the results suggest that three major ancient continental regions (Laurentia (modern North America), Baltica (northern Europe) and North China were gradually pushed up during the Neoproterozoic Era, approximately one billion to 540 million years ago. This would have left vast areas of land exposed to weathering and erosion for long periods, allowing water, wind and other processes to wear away rock that had formed much earlier.

But removing the rock is only part of the puzzle. They also needed to explain why the gaps are still visible today.

It has been revealed that their models suggest that the same regions subsequently began to sink. As sea levels rose relative to the land, sediment accumulated over the older, eroded surfaces, creating the sharp divide between ancient and younger rocks that we can still see today.

Industry observers note that crucially, the researchers found that the timing of the simulated continental uplift and sinking was consistent with geological evidence from North America, northern Europe and North China. This suggests that movements deep within Earth's mantle may have played a major role in shaping the geological record we see today.

Recent findings suggest that daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

Sonia Bompastor’s side remain unbeaten this season but their advantage over Manchester City, who play Sunday, is only two points after failing to find a way past Khiara Keating in St Helens.

The Liverpool goalkeeper tipped over Alyssa Thompson’s shot and also denied Sandy Baltimore at full stretch in the first half, before keeping out Wieke Kaptein, Keira Walsh and Sjoeke Nusken in the second.

Liverpool had ended a five-match run without a win with victory at Brighton last weekend and they carried that confidence into the game against the league leaders to move up to eighth.

A lot of top individual performances and as a collective we really stuck to the task.

According to recent reports, "They had some chances, we had some chances - ours were probably better. And then in the second half, we didn't have the same amount because it's fatiguing to replicate that pressure and at times we didn't keep the ball well enough.

According to recent reports, “But credit to the players. I am so pleased they held on as sometimes you need that just for all your work.”.

In the late kick-off, Danielle van de Donk and Alexia Putellas both scored twice as London City Lionesses closed the gap on Chelsea with a 6-2 victory against Crystal Palace.

Alanna Kennedy and Isobel Goodwin also found the net to draw Eder Maestre’s side to within four points of the leaders.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban.
  • The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.
  • Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban.

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

It has been revealed that for players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:.

Matt Crooks - Hull City (five yellow cards).

Matty Cash - Aston Villa (five).

If any of the following players receive another Premier League yellow card before the season's halfway point, they will be banned for one match:.

Vitaly Janelt - Brentford (four).

Oli McBurnie - Hull City (four).

Harry Maguire - Manchester United (four).

Pascal Gross - Brighton & Hove Albion (four).

Ethan Ampadu - Leeds United (four).

Oliver Boscagli - Brighton & Hove Albion (four).

Adam Smith - Bournemouth (four).

Marcus Tavernier - Bournemouth (four).

Antonio Silve - Bournemouth (four).

Yeremy Pino - Crystal Palace (four).

Alexis Mac Allister - Liverpool (four).

James McAtee - Nottingham Forest (four).

The following players will miss their club's next set of fixtures:.

Max Dowman - Arsenal (red card suspension).

Jean-Philippe Mateta - Crystal Palace (red card suspension).

Igor Thiago - Brentford (red card suspension).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s fair to say that anyone would be spoilt for choice when it comes to selecting the most physical challenge of Graeme Souness’ career.

The fiery Scot was one of the most uncompromising players of his - or anyone else’s - generation, with the former Liverpool skipper taking no prisoners as he patrolled the middle of the park.

It has been revealed that but even by his standards, one challenge stands out above all. That came in a European Cup tie against Steaua Bucharest in 1987, when Liverpool welcomed the Romanian side back to Anfield.

According to recent reports, “We'd gone out there and lost the first leg 2-0,” Souness recalls to FourFourTwo. “There was a guy called Marius Lacatus who was going around topping people.

“In the second game, I thought, ‘If I get half a chance, I'll give him one.’”.

It didn’t take long for that chance to present itself.

“After about 10 minutes, I went through this guy at groin height – when he went down and rolled over, I thought, ‘I've got the wrong player…' Lacatus was 15 or 20 yards away, laughing at me because he thought I was getting sent off.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Much to Souness’ surprise, that red card didn’t come.

Recent findings suggest that “When I made the challenge, I thought, ‘F**k, I've got a problem here', so I went down as well, pretending someone had kicked me. It worked! I should have been arrested and spent time behind bars…”.

The Scot would recieve his fair share of red and yellow cards during his illustrious playing career, but as he looks back on his career, he does not regret this approach.

“The reality is that I was sent off six or seven times in my career,” he continues. “Not bad given the nature of the game in those days. Every team had a couple of people who would get involved in the physical aspect.

“At Liverpool, people didn't say, ‘Oh we're playing Liverpool today, let's have a jolly nice game of football.' It was, ‘Let's put a few of them on their backsides and see how they deal with it.' If you stood up to that and it settled into a game of football, generally we'd win.

“We could do both – we had to.”.

Graeme Souness' fresh book My Rangers is available now.

In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

Republic of Ireland have plenty of promise, but are unable to shake self-sabotage

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that the Republic of Ireland stand on the verge, although of what, nobody seems quite sure.
  • According to recent reports, for 78 minutes in Linz on Saturday, Heimir Hallgrímsson’s side gave as good as they got against an Austria side who had not lost at home for a little more than three years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hopes of promotion remain alive, but another costly collapse has raised familiar questions before the decisive Nations League game with Kosovo.

Sources indicate that the Republic of Ireland stand on the verge, although of what, nobody seems quite sure. Tuesday’s final Nations League group match, at home to Kosovo, presents a chance for progress or yet another opportunity to showcase a frustrating habit of messing things up.

According to recent reports, for 78 minutes in Linz on Saturday, Heimir Hallgrímsson’s side gave as good as they got against an Austria side who had not lost at home for a little more than three years. Set up in a compact, attack-minded formation they carried credible threat against hosts managed by Ralf Rangnick, but to nobody’s great surprise Sasa Kalajdzic broke the deadlock, scrambling home the winner from a needlessly conceded and poorly defended corner.

According to recent reports, this late lapse neatly captures the contradiction bedevilling this Ireland team under Hallgrímsson. Over the past 12 months, Ireland have been unmistakably better than they were during the dark days of the post-pandemic slump under Stephen Kenny. They have established a clear identity and pulled off a couple of phenomenal wins with a spine of players performing at an elite level, supplemented by emerging talent from the leagues below and beyond. Yet for all that, an acceptable level of success remains elusive for a team who have not managed to shake a maddening habit of self-sabotage.

They have a high ceiling, as they demonstrated a year ago. Last November they dismantled Portugal at the Aviva Stadium in a World Cup qualifier before booking their place in the playoffs with an unforgettable come-from-behind win against Hungary at the Puskas Arena.

In a recent development, in Budapest, the celebrations of a dramatic Troy Parrott hat-trick completed in the sixth minute of added time went viral and elevated the then AZ striker from being surplus to the requirements of a dreadful Tottenham to sought-after European household name. For the first time in almost a decade, Ireland were playing with something resembling swagger, spearheaded by a poster-boy striker apparently entering his prime.

Riding that wave, Ireland travelled to Prague last March for the playoff semi-final against Czechia, with Parrott striking again, from the penalty spot, as they set about taking an early 2-0 lead. What followed would become the lowest point of Hallgrímsson’s reign as Ireland sat back and invited pressure before conceding a needless penalty and subsequent late equaliser that preceded a crushing shootout defeat. Despite last summer’s expanded 48-team format in North America, poor game management had stymied Ireland’s chances of making the cut.

Sources indicate that an uninspiring, but unbeaten, summer friendly window featured fairly routine low-profile wins over Grenada and Qatar and a 1-1 draw against the World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal. Having steadied the ship before this Nations League campaign, Ireland produced a performance in their opener against Kosovo little short of diabolical and went down to another late goal.

In the subsequent four fixtures, two overshadowed by loud protests over Ireland’s decision to honour matches against Israel, that same cycle of promise and frustration has played out on a loop.

The disappointment of defeat in Pristina was immediately cancelled out by a clinical dispatch of Israel in Debrecen. In Dublin, against Austria, Parrott struck twice to give Ireland a commanding first-half lead, but in a collapse that rather mirrored their nightmarish Prague experience, Ireland went on to relinquish control and were forced to settle for a disappointing draw.

Three days later they coughed up another lead in a bad-tempered 1-1 draw with Israel, their compulsion for throwing away cheap points from winning positions coming back to bite them. Although they never led against Austria on Saturday, when Caoimhín Kelleher made a series of excellent saves, the winner they conceded was ridiculously soft.

Industry observers note that hallgrímsson’s appointment in July 2024 after a drawn-out process lasting eight months came as a surprise. He has built a side with a strong, if occasionally gaffe-prone, backbone including Kelleher, the goalkeeper’s Brentford teammate Nathan Collins and the Ipswich defender Dara O’Shea. Jack Moylan, having the season of his life at Cardiff, has impressed in midfield, and Southampton’s Finn Azaz is an occasional, but unreliable, source of creative guile. Parrott, enjoying life in La Liga with Real Betis, has evolved from promising talent to undisputed focal point of the attack.

To his credit, Hallgrímsson has forged a clear, pragmatic identity that maximises his team’s strengths without any delusions of fancy-dan footballing grandeur against elite opposition. Under his watch, Ireland are rarely outclassed and carry a cutting edge sorely absent in the dying days of his predecessor’s tenure.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, an inability to concentrate for 90 minutes continues to be their undoing and the must-win Nations League group finale at the Aviva Stadium will provide the ultimate judgment on the past 12 months. With Austria guaranteed promotion to League A, Ireland still have second place and its promotion playoff spot within reach.

Industry observers note that victory over Kosovo would also secure a place in pot two for next month’s Euro qualifying draw in Belfast, whereas defeat could leave them flirting with a relegation playoff to the tournament’s third tier. As the only ever-present residents of the Nations League’s second tier, now may be the time for something finally to give.

#71017. Can the EU make it harder to trick consumers online?

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (820 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Can the EU make it harder to trick consumers online?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA), a company would have to remind you before the free trial ends and get your explicit agreement before it can start charging you.
  • The Commission presented the proposal on Wednesday.
  • "We haven't seen that kind of reform in consumer protection in the last 20 years," Agustin Reyna, director general of the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), told DW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA), a company would have to remind you before the free trial ends and get your explicit agreement before it can start charging you. The proposed law would also make it easier to cancel a subscription online and require reminders before certain contracts renew automatically.

The Commission presented the proposal on Wednesday. It wants to give consumers more control over how much time and money they spend online.

"We haven't seen that kind of reform in consumer protection in the last 20 years," Agustin Reyna, director general of the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), told DW.

His organization pushed for stronger EU rules against manipulative online practices. He sees the proposal as a good starting point for tackling problems that frustrate consumers every day.

The proposal also includes a ban on manipulative marketing tactics, so-called "dark patterns." A concrete example: You are trying to reserve a hotel room and the website claims that only three are left, a potentially false claim to pressure you into buying.

A concert ticket that gets more expensive while you're waiting in an online queue raises a different problem. The price could still go up in the process, but the seller would have to show the current price while you wait and tell you the maximum you could be asked to pay.

Online games that encourage people to spend their money to advance are also targeted. Children would no longer be able to pay to win or get to the next level of their online game.

It has been revealed that marketing and personalized ads would need to be clearly marked and restricted in the case of children. Consumers should get the option to switch off doomscrolling functions such as the autoplay of videos, showing one clip after the other. With these fresh rules, the EU wants to make apps and websites less addictive.

Industry observers note that for Christoph Busch, an academic with a focus on consumer law and digital services based at Osnabrück University in Germany, the option to opt out doesn't go far enough. He argues that a version in which consumers actively have to choose to opt into those functions would be more effective.

In a recent development, "But then there is always the question of proportionality," Busch mentioned. "And I think here the European legislators are trying to balance different interests.".

These competing interests are particularly visible in the gaming industry, where interest groups have warned that the proposed EU restrictions could hurt developers and leave players with fewer options to choose from.

Video Games Europe and the European Games Developer Federation called the proposal "unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate," arguing that a ban on selling children features that help them win or advance is worded so broadly that it "could cover almost any purchase in a game.".

According to recent reports, for Busch, this argument doesn't hold. "If your business model is based on addictive design features, then maybe your business model has to be reviewed," he said.

Catalina Goanta, an associate professor of private law and technology at Utrecht University, emphasized in an interview with DW that "regulation can very easily slide into overregulation.".

According to recent reports, even though she believes that the DFA is a solid and reasonable compromise, she argues that prohibiting dark patterns and doomscrolling altogether would be too prohibitive. Many of the concerns consumers currently face could be resolved by enforcing existing regulation more effectively, she noted.

She points to the fact that the EU has made a name for itself in the past by adding newly introduced rules and regulations that have made it more difficult to access the European market, especially for small online businesses.

BEUC director Agustin Reyna disagrees.

"Instead of having 27 different regulations to adhere to, companies will now only get one," Reyna stated.

For him, this speaks for simplification, especially when the responsibility for compliance is shared between online influencers and the platforms they publish on.

According to the new legislation, the EU would have the possibility to impose fines of up to six percent of a company's global annual revenue should the company violate the law.

According to recent reports, the European Parliament and the Council, which represents member state governments, still have to agree on the text and formally adopt it. All experts agree that in that process, changes are still very likely.

It has been revealed that "It will be a difficult trialogue, especially in this climate of simplification and deregulation with a focus on strengthening European competitiveness," mentioned Christoph Busch. In that climate, it is not easy to add consumer rights, he adds.

Agustin Reyna is more optimistic. "The parliament is a divided house, much more than in the past," he notes. "But consumer protection is a subject that brings parties together because it brings tangible outcomes to people.".

#71014. Chelsea’s deep and ongoing issues revealed by Leeds drubbing

Chelsea’s deep and ongoing issues revealed by Leeds drubbing

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
  • By the end, amid what Xabi Alonso described as a “fragile moment”, even his own cultured touch had deserted him.
  • He’s now seeing his reputation as a coach plummet, as Chelsea fall to eighth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

By the end, amid what Xabi Alonso described as a “fragile moment”, even his own cultured touch had deserted him. As his Chelsea team tried to offer something in the final minutes of an utterly nothing performance against a brilliant Leeds United, the ball was easily cleared for a throw. Alonso, famed for his technique as a player, miscontrolled it towards his underwhelming bench.

He’s now seeing his reputation as a coach plummet, as Chelsea fall to eighth. This 4-1 evisceration was not just Leeds’ first win at the home of their old Seventies rivals since 1999 – to add to how Tottenham Hotspur also won here a few weeks ago – but a second defeat in a row, and a fifth in 11 this season.

And yet the very nature of it was still worse than any numbers can tell.

Outside an early Emmanuel Emegha goal on his first start, there was nothing to speak positively about, and just nothing about Chelsea.

Leeds found it easy to get at them, and they were soon rampaging through them.

They could have been 3-1 up by half-time, after Noah Okafor’s well-taken equaliser, but it never looked like it would take long to get there in the second half.

And, sure, Chelsea might well dispute the absurd-looking handball decision that eventually gave Dominic Calvert-Lewin his goal to make it 2-1, but they couldn’t dispute that it was coming.

Recent findings suggest that leeds were rampant, Okafor soon lashing in his second from yet another poorly-defended set-piece. There, Austin MacPhee’s influence becomes just one more aspect to question about the first team.

The manner of Brenden Aaronson’s goal, as he was allowed to just surge through the team, summed the afternoon up.

Chelsea didn’t look a team. Leeds, by contrast, knew exactly what they were about in every moment of the game. They had an identity.

Chelsea are instead looking to individuals.

They lost all cohesion once Moises Caicedo again went off injured, having already lacked any bite without Joao Pedro.

The striker was nevertheless involved in what might actually have been one of the match’s most telling moments.

As Cole Palmer went off, Chelsea coach Willie Isa seemed to gesture the forward towards the fans.

According to recent reports, there were admittedly very few left, and many of those had loudly booed on the final whistle. Palmer didn’t go over, and then seemed to have a few words with Joao Pedro, too.

They didn’t look all that amicable.

“We were disappointed,” Alonso stated afterwards.

Either way, there is probably a bigger point there, that emphasises how all this is bigger than the manager.

Yes, a coach as accomplished as Alonso should be doing better than this. There has been constant talk that some of the players haven’t found him as tactically sophisticated as they expected, something which has arguably manifested in how they seem to have got worse the more time he’s had with them – in the same way they got worse the longer this game went on.

To apparently have such little fight, and lose the club’s two biggest grudge matches at home for the first time in 67 years, is awful to have on your CV.

Sources indicate that the kind of fight that can preserve that kind of record, however, comes from something deeper. It comes from culture.

In a recent development, it’s why there’s almost a symbolism in Isa having that word with Palmer after the game, given that the coach is seen as a “cultural architect”. One of his qualities is building the right mood at a club.

But how do you really do that when everything is changing all the time?

So, yes, Chelsea could reasonably ask questions of the manager. Fans already sound like they might want him out.

But it’s still just 11 games, in a situation where there has been constant upheaval.

Recent findings suggest that only eight regular Chelsea squad members have been there for three years or more. The longest-serving after the home-grown Reece James – again out today – and Levi Colwell is Wesley Fofana.

He’s been here since 2022, but has also been injured so often, to the point it’s hard not to wonder whether it’s prevented him reaching the performance level he is capable of.

And all of that as other signings have constantly swirled around them.

Yes, Chelsea may have recently made moves to address this, as illustrated with the signings of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck.

You can’t just buy in culture, though. It isn’t plug in and play. It has to be developed over a long period, with, yes, individuals setting standards.

Recent findings suggest that one or two players can’t do that on their own. There has to be something more.

Recent findings suggest that there has to be something that a head coach can fit into, that he can amplify. Of course, Alonso has been named as a manager rather than head coach, because the job is so much bigger.

No wonder Chelsea are “fragile”, or struggling to recover when they “receive a punch”, as Alonso put it.

You withstand that through resilience, which comes from culture, which comes from principles.

Industry observers note that chelsea haven’t had any of that applied, really, since Thomas Tuchel. No coach has had enough time, either in the job or with a defined core of players.

The ebullient Daniel Farke, by contrast, knows his squad inside out. He was able to laugh about how the music they were playing – pumping through the away dressing-room wall – is a bit too loud for him.

His team ensured the visiting fans made plenty of noise. They knew exactly what they were about, because they know exactly what they are. They have an identity.

In a recent development, they closed Chelsea out when needed, and boxed them in when they wanted. It made the final score… inevitable. And yet, it could have been worse.

Alonso needs more than coaching to make this get better.

#71013. Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid

Echoes of Azteca but not like Argentina: fearless England start afresh in Madrid

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1193 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • ‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics.
  • Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead.
  • The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics.

Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2. The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before.

The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he remarked, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards.

It has been revealed that against Mexico, the defender was sent off for a late tackle in the 54th minute with England 2-1 up. Against Spain, he contributed to Elliot Anderson being sent off in the 63rd minute with England 3-0 up. Quansah had his pocket picked by Lamine Yamal and Anderson’s attempt to chase back and rectify the situation ended with him fouling the winger.

According to recent reports, it was not only a red card but a penalty; the prompt for Spain to launch a furious and hitherto unadvertised fightback. It had the stand that housed the press box shaking. Structural integrity was very much a theme.

As in Mexico, Tuchel made defensive changes. This time, it was Myles Lewis-Skelly for Harry Kane; Djed Spence for Anthony Gordon. Tuchel also withdrew Jude Bellingham, who went off shaking his head. It was easy to understand his frustration. He was excellent. Tuchel had removed his two prime attackers. He also put Dan Burn on towards the end, albeit this time not as part of a back five. England stayed in a 4-4-1 formation, with Quansah moving from central defence to right-back. As in Mexico, the 10-man low block resisted.

Industry observers note that as much as Tuchel disagreed, this felt like Argentina reloaded as well. “No, not at all,” he remarked, when the World Cup semi-final defeat was raised. “Because of one man down. We would not have been in this situation if it was 11 against 11.”.

It has been revealed that the parallels, nevertheless, were there. Tuchel made defensive substitutions at 1-0 up against Argentina; it was a back five on that occasion. As against Spain, his team could not get out and they faced a flurry of chances. There were other factors in play at the World Cup, chief among them the high levels of fatigue within the squad. England could not hold out, conceding two late goals to exit and bring down a wave of criticism on Tuchel.

Industry observers note that the score is the ultimate takeaway. It can skew analysis. Had Trafford not got back up after parrying a shot from the Spain substitute Fermín López to brilliantly repel Aymeric Laporte’s follow‑up, England would have gone from enjoying a fabulous result to stewing over an opportunity missed. The stakes were nowhere near as high as at the World Cup, but they would have gone from finishing top of their Nations League group to advancing into the quarter-finals as an unseeded second-place team.

In terms of Tuchel’s approach to the closing stages of a big game, what changed?

The truth for England lay in the opening 63 minutes. This was where the evidence of a decisive shift could be found, the reasons for the swell of optimism. England have never played better under Tuchel – and this was against the team to beat; the world and European champions. On their turf.

Spain were without the injured Rodri and Dani Olmo, and Luis de la Fuente strangely decided to use Pedri only as a substitute, but their lineup still shimmered with menace; Lamine Yamal was frightening. Yet before their penalty, converted by Mikel Oyarzabal, they did not have a shot on target. Or a real chance.

It has been revealed that what stood out from the first whistle was England’s front‑foot intent; the bravery on the ball. They believed they would win and there was a fearlessness about them. They made forward moves on the half turn. There was a slickness about their combinations.

Spain have never suffered like this under De la Fuente and it was everything Tuchel had dreamed of when he started to plot a latest version of his team after the World Cup; a more fluid game model, a response to the Argentina defeat.

It has been revealed that tuchel loved England’s buildup play, which included some of Trafford’s passing. He loved the high press; the aggression in the duels; the threat on set pieces. He stated he loved the low-block defending too. Ben White was excellent at right-back and there was a coming-of-age performance from Lewis Hall at left-back, but it felt wrong to single out individuals.

It has been revealed that “We didn’t stop and I think we are ready to go [like this] for 90 minutes,” Tuchel said. “It was a complete performance and we will not look back now. Go forward and stay hungry. We will not go back on this way of playing that we find ourselves since the World Cup.”.

Ezri Konsa, who headed in the second goal from a Declan Rice corner, noted England “would have scored two more” if they had kept 11 men on the pitch. “You saw until the red card how much quality we had,” he said.

It has been revealed that “We dominated the game. The instruction was to keep going at them. Don’t stop. To keep our foot on the pedal. Argentina was different; different circumstances.”.

Tuchel was asked about the journey from the heartbreak of Argentina to this point; the end of a stirring Nations League group campaign, including the 7-0 win against Croatia in Rijeka. It has not all been super exciting; the 2-1 Wembley win against Croatia last Thursday, for example, was a grind. Was he always confident of a successful reboot?

According to recent reports, “It took me a while to digest [the World Cup] and see the way forward,” he said. “How we can help and adjust and improve? We had reviews and so on but the clarity came in the first Nations League camp [in September and October] with the players.

According to recent reports, “The first week was not so easy. Some players were still upset from the World Cup. Some were newly introduced in the team. Some had digested it, some had not. But it was important to have this process together and everyone committed to wanting to improve in certain aspects of the game.

Sources indicate that “We had the energy right to take the next steps and from there we went. Full credit to the players, how they buy in. It’s amazing that it came together like this now.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

England are a seeded side for the Nations League quarter-finals after topping their group.

The draw for the final eight teams in the 2026-27 Nations League will be on Friday, 20 November at 11:00 GMT.

It will take place at Uefa's headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland and be broadcast on Uefa TV.

England are the only home nation to have made it to the quarter-final stage, however Northern Ireland's draw against Hungary saw them top Group B2 and secure promotion to League A in the 2028-29 tournament.

Scotland will remain in League B following their third-place finish in Group B1, and Wales face a League A/B relegation play-off in March after being consigned to last place in Group A4.

The Republic of Ireland finished second in Group B3 and so will take part in a League A/B promotion play-off in March.

The winners of groups A1-A4 are seeded for the draw, playing the runners-up of other groups in League A.

England have sealed their place in the last eight as Group A3 winners and could face:.

They cannot face A3 runners-up Spain as teams must be drawn against sides from other groups.

The quarter-finals will be played over two legs during the international break between 25-30 March.

Seeded teams get to play the second leg of their quarter-final at home.

Nations that reach the semi-finals can bid those penultimate matches as well as the final.

The remaining dates for the Nations League are:.

Quarter-finals first leg: 25-27 March.

Quarter-finals second leg: 28-30 March.

Semi-finals, third-place play-off and final: 9-13 June.

On this day in space! Nov. 18, 2013: NASA launches MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to find out how the Red Planet lost its water

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on Nov.
  • The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN.
  • Industry observers note that MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars.

The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago.

Industry observers note that MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars. The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result.

Recent findings suggest that solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere. Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere once kept Mars warm enough to sustain liquid water on its surface, and losing that greenhouse gas turned Mars into a cold and dry place.

NASA's MAVEN spacecraft was the first Mars orbiter ever built to measure how the Martian atmosphere interacts with solar wind, as well as how that constant stream of particles from the sun slowly stripped the Red Planet of its precious atmosphere over time.

After its launch in 2013, MAVEN spent about 10 months en route to Mars before entering orbit on Sept. 21, 2014. The spacecraft then spent the better part of 11 years studying the Red Planet from orbit using three different suites of instruments: An imaging ultraviolet spectrograph to study the global characteristics of the Martian atmosphere; a Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectromenter to measure its composition; and a six-instrument setup to study how Mars' ionosphere reacts to solar wind.

"The science MAVEN has given us is key to informing what kind of radiation protection and safety measures we must take before sending humans to Mars," Louise Prockter, NASA director of planetary science, said in June 2026 after the mission concluded. "The data collected from MAVEN will continue to provide valuable insight into Mars for decades to come.".

MAVEN was originally designed to study Mars for 1 full Earth year after arriving at the Red Planet. That mission ended in 2016, but the spacecraft managed to survive for another 10 years adding more observations for scientists to study.

In a recent development, NASA ultimately began using MAVEN as a communications relay for other missions at Mars as the orbiter aged. In December 2025, MAVEN went silent, with NASA losing communication with the orbiter.

In a recent development, an investigation later found that the probe sent its final signal on Dec. 6, 2025 as it was heading behind Mars (as seen from Earth). But when it emerged on the other side, it had gone into an uncontrollable spin that led to a loss of power, dooming the spacecraft.

NASA tried in vain to recover the spacecraft over several months, ultimately declaring the mission over in June 2026.

According to recent reports, "Best. Mars. Mission. Ever," Shannon Curry, MAVEN's principal investigator, stated of the probe's entire 12.5-year mission when it ended. The team "really experienced the loss of a loved one with the end of the mission here.".

Hanneke Weitering is a multimedia journalist in the Pacific Northwest reporting on the future of aviation at FutureFlight.aero and Aviation International News and was previously the Editor for Spaceflight and Astronomy news here at Space.com. As an editor with over 10 years of experience in science journalism she has previously written for Scholastic Classroom Magazines, MedPage Today and The Joint Institute for Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. After studying physics at the University of Tennessee in her hometown of Knoxville, she earned her graduate degree in Science, Health and Environmental Reporting (SHERP) from New York University. Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. In her spare time, Hanneke enjoys exploring the Rocky Mountains, basking in nature and looking for dark skies to gaze at the cosmos.

#71006. Industry News: Noni Madueke rescues Arsenal and salvages point against inspired Newcastle

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (649 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Noni Madueke rescues Arsenal and salvages point against inspired Newcastle

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (649 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later?
  • Noni Madueke snatched a 2-2 draw for Arsenal after Newcastle produced a stunning second-half turnaround to claim a deserved point against the Premier League leaders.
  • Eberechi Eze put the champions in front and Madueke wasted a couple of chances to increase the lead before half-time, with Matthias Jaissle’s side jeered off following a listless first 45 minutes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Noni Madueke snatched a 2-2 draw for Arsenal after Newcastle produced a stunning second-half turnaround to claim a deserved point against the Premier League leaders.

Eberechi Eze put the champions in front and Madueke wasted a couple of chances to increase the lead before half-time, with Matthias Jaissle’s side jeered off following a listless first 45 minutes.

They rallied in stunning fashion on the resumption, with Harvey Barnes scoring Newcastle’s first goal at St James’ Park since September 19 before Malick Thiaw put them ahead after the hour from close range.

Former Newcastle captain Bruno Guimaraes underwhelmed on his return to Tyneside, his every touch booed before he was brought off after 70 minutes, but his latest employers claimed a share of the spoils thanks to Madueke.

Arsenal’s five-match winning run in the league was halted, although they extended their lead at the top of the table to six points over second-placed Brighton, who could halve the deficit at Hull on Sunday.

Newcastle came into the fixture with significant concerns about where their goals were coming from and they were up against the most miserly defence in the league, with Arsenal conceding just five times in their previous 10 games.

Newcastle were given an early warning when Madueke cut inside and left England team-mate Dan Burn trailing in his wake, with the Arsenal forward’s low shot to the near post hitting the outside of it.

Arsenal’s press meant there was no let-up for Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, who made a series of distribution errors, and it was a heart-in-mouth moment for the home side’s fans when Guimaraes got ahead of Barnes but the Brazilian could not direct a sliding volley on-target.

The Magpies’ luck ran out in the 33rd minute when Kai Havertz dispossessed Lewis Hall before sliding a perfectly-weighted pass to Eze, who went in behind Amar Dedic to finish coolly past Hornicek.

Matters might have worsened before half-time as more loose play allowed Madueke to pick his pocket. Madueke bore down on goal but took one touch too many before his shot was saved by Hornicek.

Hall made partial amends to then deny Madueke’s shot while Eze’s free-kick was saved as Arsenal ended the half on top, prompting Jaissle to make a triple substitution at the break, with Jacob Ramsey, Anthony Elanga and Tino Livramento replacing Jacob Murphy and Dedic and Sean Steur.

Newcastle exploded out of the traps and needed just four minutes after the restart to draw level, with Martin Odegaard nudged off the ball by Joe Willock and the ball dropping to William Osula, who teed up Barnes to fire beyond David Raya with aplomb.

It was Newcastle’s first goal at home in 312 minutes and with the crowd now firmly behind them, they remarkably took the lead with Arsenal at sixes and sevens.

The unmarked Burn headed Hall’s corner on-target and a goalmouth scramble between Willock and Arsenal duo Gabriel and Raya led to Thiaw poking home from a yard out in the 62nd minute.

Arteta was forced into a substitution with Raya suffering a shoulder injury, while Guimaraes was also hooked alongside Eze with 20 minutes to go to the delight of Newcastle’s supporters as Kepa Arrizabalaga, Christos Tzolis and Myles Lewis-Skelly were introduced.

Newcastle continued to pile forward but were undone in the 78th minute when a fluid move forwards from Arsenal ended with Madueke cutting onto his left foot and dispatching through Hornicek’s hands and in.

Both sides had chances to claim victory in a frenzied atmosphere but neither could manage another breakthrough before Guimaraes, the first Newcastle captain to lift a trophy in 56 years following their historic 2025 Carabao Cup triumph, was cheered at full-time when he completed a lap of the pitch.

#71003. Tech Report: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (942 w)

Tech Report: Thomas Frank’s to-do list: lift mood, fix defence and fire up Sarr and Mateta

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead.
  • Sources indicate that thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long.
  • Sources indicate that frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Seeking redemption after failing at Spurs, newly installed Crystal Palace manager has a tough challenge ahead.

Sources indicate that thomas Frank promised his wife, Nanna, he would take a year’s sabbatical after being sacked by Tottenham in February, but he couldn’t wait that long. Having received a reported £8m payoff from Spurs, he kept an extremely low profile in the first few months after an experience at the club that sources close to the 53‑year‑old have described as “traumatic”.

Sources indicate that frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. It noted he would cover the World Cup for the BBC (thereby going head-to-head with Ange Postecoglou, his predecessor at Spurs, who worked for ITV) before “experiencing the Tour de France”, a lifelong passion. Frank usually preferred to run to Brentford’s training ground and home matches from his home in East Sheen during a nine‑year spell as assistant and then manager, but he occasionally cycled because it helped to clear his head.

Industry observers note that by the time the statement was released the Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, is understood to have sounded out Frank out over his willingness to take over from Oliver Glasner. But it confirmed his intention to keep his promise and not rush back into management. “When the time is right, I will look forward to my return as a manager, ready to embrace the job with great energy and dedication,” he stated.

In a recent development, with Palace facing the prospect of ending a 14-season stay in the Premier League – the eighth‑longest in the division – after a dreadful start under Pierre Sage, that time has arrived. Frank left Tottenham with a win ratio of 34.2% – the worst of any permanent manager in the club’s history – but has the chance to redeem himself at a club he is said to have admired from afar.

According to the biography Thomas Frank: The Premier League Diaries, by the Danish author Kasper Steenbach, published last year, Frank attended the 2025 FA Cup final victory against Manchester City with a childhood friend from Denmark who supports Palace after arranging tickets for him. Frank is mentioned to have been impressed by the atmosphere for which Selhurst Park has become renowned. That said, the absence of the influential supporters’ group the Holmesdale Fanatics since it disbanded at the start of the season has made it less intimidating for visiting teams.

Industry observers note that nonetheless, Frank is noted to be itching to return to the dugout after failing at Spurs, where he inherited a squad that had just won the Europa League under Postecoglou but struggled to impose himself at a club with higher expectations. Frank’s preference to play on the counterattack with a more direct style looks a better fit at Palace, although his critics will question whether his success at Brentford was really down to the system put in place by the club’s owner, Matthew Benham, that has allowed Keith Andrews to thrive since the former set-piece coach stepped into Frank’s shoes.

It has been revealed that there is no such framework in place at Palace, with their longevity in the Premier League mainly down to a series of shrewd managerial appointments at the right time by Parish which have ensured they have not finished lower than 15th since being promoted in 2013. Frank, who is also understood to have attracted interest from Denmark in the summer and Newcastle and Fulham in recent weeks after difficult starts for Matthias Jaissle and Álvaro Arbeloa respectively, will be expected to make an immediate impression.

In a recent development, for now he must make do with a squad seriously lacking in leaders after the sales of Marc Guéhi, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Muñoz this year. Frank’s first task must be to instil some defensive discipline in a side who have conceded 24 goals in 10 league games.

His Brentford side were renowned for their organisation and prowess from set pieces, an area Palace have struggled with for several seasons. He will have to tread carefully if he intends to impose the “no dickheads” policy he borrowed from the All Blacks during his time as Brentford manager.

Sage’s attempts to impose himself on the squad by dropping the defenders Jaydee Canvot and Axel Disasi for poor performances and indiscipline respectively backfired because his team kept losing, not to mention that it angered Parish. Frank, who is believed to have been offered assurances that Palace will bring in defensive reinforcements in January, faces a delicate balancing act with a squad desperately low on morale.

The futures of Ismaïla Sarr and Jean‑Philippe Mateta could be key to Palace’s prospects of avoiding the drop. Sarr was the club’s player of the year when they won the Conference League last season but he played only 107 minutes in the Premier League under Sage owing to a groin injury. The Senegal forward’s head was turned by interest from Liverpool in the summer and Frank will have to rely on his best motivational skills to get the best out of him and Mateta, who is suspended for crucial games against Coventry and Hull after his red card against Tottenham.

The France striker tried to annul the final year of his contract after a move to Milan was scuppered by a failed medical in January and he is likely to push for a move again. But he remains popular in the dressing room and could be the talisman for Palace’s survival push if Frank can persuade him that the grass may not be greener.

#71002. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 2 min read (475 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.
  • Recent findings suggest that the group known as OPEC+ confirmed Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year.
  • Recent findings suggest that the production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

Recent findings suggest that the group known as OPEC+ confirmed Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

Recent findings suggest that the production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”.

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

It has been revealed that “We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts.

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

According to recent reports, kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US prepares additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he noted.

EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (844 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.
  • The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.

Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.

"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.

But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.

Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.

"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations.".

Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.

"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.

European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.

Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa stated in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.

Putin noted a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove fresh joiners Finland and Sweden, could be among his demands.

It has been revealed that "What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately.".

This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of, especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.

"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," stated Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. "If something is a threat to you, will you discuss your defense with the threat [itself]?".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US President Donald Trump stated publicly that he was hoping for a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe.".

Zelensky noted he found the US approach "a bit strange.".

Many of Europe's leaders speaking in Dublin referenced previous agreements with Russia that they believe Moscow has breached.

They include the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter, 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the one they consider most crucial: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which forbids Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defense.

The rancor over the seat at the peace talks is drawing focus away from arguably the bigger battle in the EU now ― how to fund Ukraine as the war continues.

Back in October, the European Commission identified a €70 billion hole in the EU’s funding it had promised for Ukraine’s economy.

Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico has opposed any further financial and military support for Ukraine.

But Germany's Merz warned he could block the EU's next seven-year budget unless member states agree to contribute to Ukraine's financing.

Dundee United made history with a landmark 4-0 demolition of Hibernian.

Hearts returned to winning ways in spectacular style as they destroyed 10-man Dundee 8-0 at Dens.

#70996. How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1683 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

How to turn impostor syndrome into a superpower

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers.
  • In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.
  • For Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, Upcoming Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Impostor syndrome — a fear of being less competent than people think — is common in researchers. Credit: Gandee Vasan/Getty.

In 2021, Kwabena Boahen Asare found himself in at the deep end when he joined a skin cancer laboratory to gain hands-on research experience.

For Asare, who was a first-year undergraduate student at Dartmouth College in Hanover, Upcoming Hampshire, at the time, it was an exciting but daunting prospect. Not only was he the sole bachelor’s programme student working alongside senior researchers with years of experience under their belts, he was also the only Black person in the lab. Although Asare’s mentor and colleagues were supportive and encouraging, he felt overwhelmed and out of his depth. “There was a steep learning curve,” he states.

At the time, Asare viewed his struggles as a sign that he didn’t belong in research. This feeling was compounded by the fact that he was surrounded by colleagues who didn’t share his background as a first-generation student from Ghana.

Recent findings suggest that his experience, and those of many like him, is commonly labelled as impostor syndrome — the fear of not being as competent or knowledgeable as other people think, despite objective accomplishments. In a world that often prizes unflinching self-confidence and boldness, impostor syndrome is usually cast as a psychological flaw that the individual needs to ‘fix’. But it can be a natural response to working in a challenging environment or striving towards an ambitious goal, organizational psychologists say.

In a recent development, impostor syndrome can also be a reaction to systemic bias and exclusion in the workplace, particularly for people from under-represented groups, including women, says Ruchika Malhotra, an inclusion strategist and founder of Candour, a workplace consultancy in Seattle, Washington. The tech giant advises organizations on strategies to create diverse teams and inclusive cultures. One study1 conducted at universities in the United States found that women who work in scientific fields that particularly value intellectual brilliance are more likely to feel like impostors than are their male colleagues.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

How I tackled post-PhD impostor syndrome.

Much of the discussion about impostor syndrome pathologizes healthy self-doubt and shifts the responsibility onto individuals instead of the environments that exclude and marginalize them in the first place, adds Malhotra. “A lot of the ways that it’s been talked about haven’t been constructive,” she says.

Although it comes with drawbacks, in some situations, impostor syndrome can be beneficial. For instance, it can help people be better prepared and more focused, particularly when they have a long to-do list.

“Impostor thoughts are almost like your superpower when things get pretty overwhelming,” says Basima Tewfik, an organizational psychologist who studies impostor syndrome at Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge.

Looking back, Asare says that his impostor syndrome prompted him to reflect on why he wanted to become a researcher in the first place. It has also made him more conscious of his resilience, how he needs to improve and when to seek help, as well as giving him more empathy. This has made him better able to support younger students and researchers who are feeling out of place. “It became my strength,” says Asare, who is now an oncology researcher and consultant at Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center in Lebanon, New Hampshire.

Impostor syndrome was first described as ‘impostor phenomenon’ in a 1978 paper on high-achieving women2 co-authored by psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes, both then at Georgia State University in Atlanta. They wrote that people who experience this phenomenon “maintain a strong belief that they are not intelligent; in fact they are convinced that they have fooled anyone who thinks otherwise”.

In the decades since, impostor phenomenon has morphed into a syndrome, even though it isn’t a medical diagnosis, nor is it classified as a psychiatric disorder. A review published in 20233 suggests that around 70% of people will feel unworthy of their accomplishments at some point in their lives. These feelings are even more prevalent in academia, with a 2012 study4 finding that as many as 82% of graduate students experience impostor syndrome to at least some degree. This pattern of thinking often affects high achievers and is associated with lower job satisfaction, hindered performance and burnout. Although some studies, including the 2012 paper, suggest that impostor syndrome affects mostly women and people from other groups under-represented in academia, others argue that it arises in specific situations rather than among particular groups. Relatively few studies have investigated whether commonly cited strategies, such as listing one’s accomplishments and accepting compliments from others, are actually effective.

Impostor syndrome has become a catchphrase in popular culture, with dozens of articles, books and courses describing what it is and how people can overcome it. But in the scientific literature, at least, the exact definition of impostor syndrome, or phenomenon, varies widely. This has created a murky picture of what it really is and how it affects people, claims Tewfik. “There are a lot of different ways people describe this phenomenon,” she says. The loose definition has made it easy to confuse impostor syndrome, which causes people to make inferences about what other people think of them, with regular self-doubt, which is more of a personal reflection of your own capabilities, according to Tewfik.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

‘Maybe I was never meant to be in science’: how impostor syndrome seizes scientist mothers.

Industry observers note that much of the research on impostor syndrome has also used measures that have made it difficult to distinguish from other psychological patterns, such as negative affectivity, a personality trait that is linked to a tendency to experience negative emotions such as fear, anxiety and insecurity, adds Tewfik. This crossover might explain why most studies on impostor syndrome have shown only negative outcomes, such as a lack of career planning and low motivation to lead5. “It’s possible that what we’ve been studying is actually something much more akin to fear,” claims Tewfik.

This overly negative slant is exacerbated by the fact that many workplaces, including academic ones, place too much emphasis on self-confidence, indicates Tomas Chamorro-Premuzic, an organizational psychologist at University College London. One 2024 study6 found that workers who display confidence are perceived as more competent and dominant, irrespective of their actual ability.

If impostor syndrome hinders a person’s ability to work or form relationships, it’s usually a symptom of a deeper issue or clinical condition, such as an anxiety disorder. But feeling like you’re about to be ‘found out’ before delivering a big presentation, for example, is usually a sign that you’re being challenged or working outside your comfort zone, claims Chamorro-Premuzic. “There is a very healthy degree somewhere that we’re not appreciating,” he adds (see ‘A toolkit for working with impostor syndrome’).

Sources indicate that in scientists, impostor thoughts can simply be a by-product of thinking critically and approaching things with a healthy dose of scepticism, claims Samantha Sutton, an independent career coach for scientists in Boston, Massachusetts. It’s also often a natural response to working in a high-achieving, competitive environment or towards an ambitious goal and should be normalized instead of treated as a problem to solve, she adds. “If you’re up against something significant, you should be scared,” says Sutton. When she communicates this to her clients, they are often relieved to hear that they don’t need to strive for total self-confidence before taking steps towards their goals. “They realize that nothing is wrong,” adds Sutton.

#70994. Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation

Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a latest study reports.
  • Sources indicate that as stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby.
  • Recent findings suggest that "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in Upcoming York, told Space.com.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a latest study reports.

Sources indicate that as stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now.

Recent findings suggest that "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in Upcoming York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect.".

Industry observers note that in the fresh study, the researchers investigated a red giant star designated WNTR23bzdiq, which is located about 2.5 million light-years away in the Andromeda galaxy. The star is about seven times heftier and 350 times wider than our own sun.

It has been revealed that in 2023, using NASA's now-defunct NEOWISE space telescope and the WINTER telescope at Palomar Observatory in California, the scientists noticed that this star was brightening. By analyzing previous records, they found that the red giant had gradually started growing more luminous in 2018.

The researchers had previously suggested this brightening potentially occurred because the giant star engulfed a companion star. As this companion spiraled toward the giant's core, it would generate friction, heat and light, explaining the increasing luminosity.

Then, near the end of 2025, the astronomers saw a giant eruption of light from this giant star. NASA's James Webb Space Telescope observed the star just 47 days after that eruption, allowing the team to characterize the event in detail. The researchers now propose that this explosion happened when a companion star about 70% the sun's mass rammed into the giant's heart.

"I was absolutely flabbergasted when we saw this," Karambelkar mentioned.

Industry observers note that in the upcoming study, the scientists estimated that the eruption expelled an amount of material equal to about 0.1 to 0.2 times the mass of the sun. "Stars engulfing their companions have been theorized for many decades, and this event provides the first observations of this theoretical prediction," Karambelkar noted.

Recent findings suggest that although these findings suggest that two stars — a binary system nicknamed "Bao" — merged into one, "it is not the only possibility," Karambelkar said. "The other possibility is that both stars survived, in a much shorter orbit. In order to conclusively determine what happened, we need to continue monitoring what the system does, once the heft of the eruption settles down.".

Now that astronomers may have found the first such merger, "I can't wait to find more," Karambelkar stated. "Upcoming telescopes like the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Vera Rubin Observatory will be very useful in discovering many more such events.".

According to recent reports, the scientists detailed their findings Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

In a recent development, charles Q. Choi is a contributing writer for Space.com and Live Science. He covers all things human origins and astronomy as well as physics, animals and general science topics. Charles has a Master of Arts degree from the University of Missouri-Columbia, School of Journalism and a Bachelor of Arts degree from the University of South Florida. Charles has visited every continent on Earth, drinking rancid yak butter tea in Lhasa, snorkeling with sea lions in the Galapagos and even climbing an iceberg in Antarctica. Visit him at http://www.sciwriter.us.

#70993. Danny Kelly loved football and never forgot the absurdity of earning a living talking about it | Max Rushden

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1241 w)
